CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL (round 1). Audited commit fafacd7 on branch devteam2/sprint-5, worktree clean, sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict. Seven of eight requirements met, several of them well. Req 7 is not met.

SPRINT FILE INTEGRITY: the commit deletes docs/sprints/1-todo/sprint-5...md, which looked alarming in the diffstat. It is a stale duplicate left behind by /sprint-start; the 2-in-progress copy is present at HEAD and I diffed the two - they differ by exactly one line, the frontmatter status field. No requirement text was altered. The in-progress file has not changed since f523f70.

BLOCKING ISSUE - Req 7 - lib/client-ip.ts lines 23-37
The requirement says read the client IP from the header Vercel actually sets rather than trusting a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For it could spoof, and my criterion is to confirm a client-supplied value cannot override it. I cannot confirm that, and the code contains nothing that would make it true - it takes the first entry of x-forwarded-for on trust.
Two separate problems, one of which is platform-independent and demonstrable on its own:
(a) PRECEDENCE IS INVERTED, and this needs no assumption about Vercel at all. When both headers are present the code prefers x-forwarded-for, a multi-value header that by convention accumulates entries, over x-real-ip, a single value a proxy sets. Demonstrated: with x-forwarded-for 9.9.9.9 and x-real-ip 203.0.113.9 present together, getClientIp returns 9.9.9.9. The file own comment cites the @vercel/functions ipAddress() helper as justification for the first-entry convention, but that helper reads x-real-ip first and falls back to x-forwarded-for. The precedence here is the reverse of the thing it cites.
(b) NO DEFENCE AGAINST AN ACCUMULATED HEADER. If any client-supplied value survives into first position, the bucket becomes attacker-chosen. Demonstrated by running the compiled module: one real client sending three different spoofed x-forwarded-for values lands in three distinct rate-limit buckets rather than one. Three buckets means the limit is not merely weakened, it is absent - a fresh allowance per request.
Being precise about what I am NOT claiming: I am not asserting that Vercel edge appends rather than replaces. I could not verify that from here and I did not try to settle it by assertion. What I can say is that the code rests entirely on that platform behaviour, states it in a comment as established fact with no evidence behind it, and nobody has tested it - the handoff verification never exercised a spoofed header. I did find one concrete data point pointing the other way for a non-Vercel deployment: Next own server does req.headers[x-forwarded-for] ??= socket.remoteAddress, which fills the header only when absent and preserves a client-supplied one verbatim. That is not production here, but it shows the assumption is not universally safe and is worth establishing rather than assuming. The sprint own Risks section names X-Forwarded-For spoofing defeats the limit trivially as a named risk whose stated mitigation is this requirement, so this is the exact thing it was written to prevent.
REQUIRED FIX - either is acceptable, both are small:
1. Prefer a header the client provably cannot influence. x-vercel-forwarded-for is Vercel-namespaced and set by the edge by construction; x-real-ip is single-valued and is what the cited helper prefers. Reading those first, with x-forwarded-for as last resort, fixes the precedence inversion outright.
2. Or keep x-forwarded-for and establish, with evidence rather than assertion, that Vercel replaces rather than appends it - and record that evidence in the comment in place of the current unsupported claim.
Either way the comment needs to stop stating the platform guarantee as a settled fact it has not demonstrated.

REQUIREMENTS COVERAGE:
Req 1: MET. RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS = 5 and RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS = 3600 as explicit named exports, with the reasoning for the choice stated where a reader finds it. No library default anywhere.
Req 2: MET, and this is the requirement the sprint exists for, so I checked it hardest. State lives in a rate_limit_hits table, one row per client per fixed window, committed as migrations/0002 with IF NOT EXISTS like 0001. The window boundary is computed inside Postgres from Postgres own now(), so instances with differing clocks converge on the same bucket without coordinating. The increment is a single atomic INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE, so two concurrent requests from one client cannot race into a lost update the way a read-then-write would. I ran the criterion grep for a module-scope Map, Set, array or counter holding limit state across lib, app and components: there is none, and none in front of the store either. The only module-scope values in the limiter are the two policy constants.
Req 3: MET. 429 with Retry-After, whose value comes from the actual window start returned by the same statement that incremented the counter, so it is consistent with the configured window by construction rather than by a second guess. Floored at 1 second so it can never tell a client to retry immediately. The body names no number, no store, and no other client.
Req 4: MET as a static fact. Five per hour against a stated normal case of about three in one sitting is real headroom. Whether it blocks genuine use is LiveQA three-ordinary-posts criterion.
Req 5: MET. The honeypot is off-screen positioned rather than display:none or a bare type=hidden, so it still looks fillable to a naive form-filler, and it carries aria-hidden true, tabIndex -1 and autoComplete off, so it is invisible, untabbable and unannounced for human, keyboard and screen-reader users alike. The field name is shared from one constant by both the form and the route handler, so the two cannot drift on what is being watched. Rejection is 400 with the same {error: string} shape as ordinary validation.
Req 6: MET, and implemented deliberately rather than by accident, which is what the requirement actually asks. The catch sets limited = false explicitly, logs the failure, and carries a comment saying in plain terms that this is a chosen trade and not to convert it to fail-closed without revisiting the requirement first. That comment is the part most likely to save this from being tidied into an outage later.
Req 8: MET. Sprint 2 validation is untouched and still runs on every path that can insert. Honeypot, then validation, then rate limit, then insert - nothing rejected at any earlier stage reaches createItem.

ON THE QUESTION DEV TEAM 2 ASKED - ordering honeypot and validation before the rate limit: your reading is right and the ordering is correct. Req 8 constrains that validation must not be weakened and that a rate-limited request must not write a row. Validation still runs ahead of every insert, so nothing is weakened, and the rate limit sits immediately before the only write it exists to gate. Not charging a client rate-limit budget for their own typos is the better behaviour, not a loophole. The one consequence worth naming out loud: honeypot-tripping and invalid traffic is never rate limited at all, so a bot can send that shape of request without bound. It costs compute and bandwidth, but no junk reaches the board, which is what this sprint set out to prevent. Worth knowing rather than worth reordering.

SIGNIFICANT RISK FOR LIVEQA, not a static defect and not blocking: checkRateLimit central SQL statement has never been executed against a real Postgres - Dev Team says so plainly, and the unit tests cover only the pure arithmetic in lib/rate-limit-window.ts. Combine that with Req 6 fail-open and the failure mode is silent: if that statement throws for any reason, posting keeps working, one log line is written, and the limiter enforces nothing while the product looks completely healthy. I read the statement closely and found no error in it - the parameter type inference through extract/floor/to_timestamp should resolve, count is usable as a column name, and the ON CONFLICT target matches the primary key - but reading is not running. LiveQA must confirm the 429 actually fires rather than inferring health from posting succeeding, and should check server logs for the fail-open line, because posting works is exactly what both a working limiter and a completely dead one look like from outside.

NON-BLOCKING:
1. Math.random appears in lib/rate-limit.ts as cleanup jitter. I checked it specifically because sprint 2 Req 3 forbids it near token generation - it is nowhere near token generation, and correctness of the limit never depends on the cleanup running. Fine, but a future grep will hit it, so it is on the record as checked.
2. Req 5 says the honeypot rejection should be indistinguishable from an ordinary validation failure. The shape is identical (400, {error}) but the message, Request could not be processed, is one no real validation rule produces. A naive bot does not read messages and a sophisticated one defeats honeypots regardless, so this changes nothing in practice - but reusing an existing validation message would make it literally identical rather than merely same-shaped.
3. Fixed window rather than sliding allows roughly double rate across a boundary. Documented in code, consistent with the sprint own framing. Accepted.
4. Unidentifiable clients share one unknown bucket rather than being exempted. That is the safe direction and is documented.

PROCESS, all correct: file ownership respected - the commit touches app/api/items/route.ts, components/board.tsx and new modules, and touches neither lib/items.ts nor app/claim/**, verified against the commit own file list rather than the handoff claim. tsconfig and package.json are shared files and were flagged for the merge rather than changed quietly; the tsconfig change is a narrow test exclusion, not a project-wide loosening, which was the right instinct. Zero new dependencies. 18 tests pass, lint exit 0, build exit 0, all run by me in the worktree.

ON THE FLAGGED CLAUDE.md INJECTION: I checked both checkouts. CLAUDE.md is unmodified in the primary checkout and in this worktree, and nothing resembling that block is present in either, so the revert held and it did not reach the commit. Flagging it rather than quietly reverting it was exactly right - a dependency writing instructions into the one file every agent here treats as authoritative is a real supply-chain concern and belongs on the record, not in a working tree someone cleans up. It is outside this sprint scope to resolve and outside mine to act on; it wants a decision from whoever owns dependency policy.

Fix Req 7, commit on this branch, and send it back - re-audit will be quick, one file. Closing note for later: this sprint closes from inside the worktree and then needs the branch and commit handed to Pipeman by name for the merge, per CLAUDE.md return path. A sprint closed in a worktree and left there reads as still open everywhere else.

PASS: PASS (round 2). Audited commit 4515ddc on branch devteam2/sprint-5, worktree clean. Sprint file re-read fresh and in full immediately before this verdict - it was amended mid-build (fee99fa), so this was a real re-read of changed requirements, not a formality. Round 1 blocker is resolved and I exercised it rather than reading it, as the amended criterion now requires.

AMENDMENT REVIEWED FIRST, since auditing a fix against stale requirements is the exact gap this step exists to close. fee99fa rewrites Req 7 into a behavioural property with three sub-parts, replaces its QA1 criterion, and adds a new LiveQA criterion. I diffed the whole sprint file across fafacd7..HEAD: Reqs 1-6 and 8, their criteria, Out of Scope and Dependencies are untouched. The only requirement text removed is Req 7 old wording, replaced by a strictly stronger version. Nothing was weakened to make the fix pass, which is the thing worth checking when a requirement changes after a FAIL.
The amendment is also, for the record, a better requirement than the one it replaces. The original named a property without naming a header or requiring the claim be evidenced, and that gap is fairly characterised in the amendment as what produced the defect. Requirements that name a behaviour and forbid a specific wrong implementation are auditable; ones that gesture at intent are not.

ROUND 1 BLOCKER RESOLVED - verified by exercise, not inspection.
7a preference order: x-vercel-forwarded-for, then x-real-ip, then x-forwarded-for as last resort. Confirmed by running the compiled module - with all three present it returns the Vercel-namespaced value; with the latter two it returns x-real-ip; x-forwarded-for wins only when alone. That is the correct order and it is no longer the reverse of the helper the comment cites.
7b leftmost never trusted: confirmed. Every one of the three headers is parsed as a potential chain and the LAST non-empty entry is taken. A header of LEFT, RIGHT resolves to RIGHT, on x-forwarded-for and on x-vercel-forwarded-for alike.
7c no unevidenced assertion: confirmed. The comment quotes Vercel current documentation with URL and date, then states explicitly that documentation is not the live measurement this sprint requires, that a static read cannot settle whether the description matches what this deployment actually receives, and that the append-versus-replace question stays open until the new LiveQA criterion runs. That is precisely what 7c asks for. Dev Team fetching the docs rather than asserting from memory was the right instinct, and not treating the docs as settling the question was the more important one.
THE BEHAVIOURAL PROPERTY, exercised directly: I replayed my own round 1 scenario against the new module. One client sending three different spoofed x-forwarded-for values, with the real address appended, now lands in ONE bucket where it previously landed in three. I then varied the attack shape seven ways - plain spoof, a multi-hop accumulated chain, a spoofed chain plus a forged x-real-ip, all three headers present, whitespace padding, a trailing comma, and leading empty entries. All seven resolve to the same single bucket. The empty-entry and trailing-comma cases matter more than they look: a naive last-entry implementation would have landed on an empty string there, and the filter in this one handles it.

REQUIREMENTS COVERAGE: Req 7 now MET. Reqs 1-6 and 8 stand exactly as recorded in round 1 - the diff since my last audit touches only lib/client-ip.ts, its test file, the sprint file and my own bookkeeping, so nothing round 1 cleared needed re-deriving. Confirmed by file list, not by assertion.

NO REGRESSION: 22 tests pass (up from 18; the new ones include a direct reproduction of my round 1 spoofing scenario), lint exit 0, build exit 0, all run by me in the worktree.

ON THE NON-BLOCKING NOTES DEV TEAM LEFT ALONE: correct call, and I would have pushed back if they had been swept up. Fixing what was raised and not refactoring adjacent code is what keeps a re-audit cheap and keeps a fix commit reviewable. All four remain open and none of them blocks anything: the honeypot rejection message being distinguishable from a real validation message, Math.random as cleanup jitter (checked, nowhere near token generation), the fixed-window double-rate boundary, and unidentified clients sharing one bucket. Address them when something else brings you into those files.

ON THE CONTAMINATED BUILD RUN: reporting that a self-verification pass was compromised and then re-running it clean is the right handling, and saying so rather than quietly presenting the second result is better still. I re-ran tests, lint and build myself from a clean worktree, so this verdict does not rest on either of your passes.

STILL FOR LIVEQA, and the two that matter most here are unchanged from round 1 plus one new:
1. The new Req 7 criterion is the only thing that can settle append-versus-replace. Vary all three headers against the real deployment after exhausting the limit, including accumulated-chain shapes, and report the header values the deployed app actually received so the answer can be cited as evidence from here on instead of assumed. Worth noting that the code now prefers x-vercel-forwarded-for above everything, so that header specifically needs to be among the ones varied - if it turns out a client can set it, the preference order makes that the most trusted input rather than the least.
2. checkRateLimit central SQL has still never executed against a real Postgres, and Req 6 fail-open makes that failure silent: if it throws, posting keeps working, one log line appears, and the limiter enforces nothing while everything looks healthy. Confirm the 429 actually fires and check server logs for the fail-open line. Posting works is what a working limiter and a completely dead one both look like from outside.
3. Req 6 own criterion about distinguishing posting failed because the database is down from posting failed because the limiter failed closed.

CLEARED for /sprint-dev-done then Pipeman. Reminder for close: this sprint closes from inside the worktree on devteam2/sprint-5, and the branch and commit then go to Pipeman by name for the merge. A sprint closed in a worktree and left there reads as still open everywhere else.

commit=ad96c1d | ci=undeterminable: could not run gh to query CI runs for ad96c1d2c775f9c831922750885597a4fe2ec0fa ([Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'gh') — gh may not be installed, or the query timed out.

FAIL: FAIL - live test round 1. The rate limit enforces NOTHING against the deployed app. One blocking defect, one lower-severity defect, and three criteria that cannot be tested until the first is fixed. Everything else runnable was run and passes.

Env: preview deployment inkr3ynq8, githubCommitSha de06441, branch devteam2/sprint-5 - app code identical to the shipped ad96c1d (git diff over the two shows only docs/sprints/state/sprint-5.json). Tested 2026-09-21 23:05-23:10 UTC with curl, real headless Chromium, and read-only SQL against Neon.

=======================================================================
DEFECT 1 - BLOCKING. The rate limit does not exist at runtime.
=======================================================================
Nine consecutive POSTs to /api/items from one client, no headers varied, against a configured limit of 5 per hour:
  post 1: HTTP 201 (id 23)   post 2: 201 (24)   post 3: 201 (25)
  post 4: HTTP 201 (id 26)   post 5: 201 (27)   post 6: 201 (28)
  post 7: HTTP 201 (id 29)   post 8: 201 (30)   post 9: 201 (31)
Zero 429s. Zero Retry-After headers on any response. All nine rows were created and all nine are on the board. Posts 6 through 9 should every one have been refused.

ROOT CAUSE, established rather than guessed:
  - The limiter's store is Postgres, table rate_limit_hits, created by the committed migration migrations/0002_create_rate_limit_hits.sql.
  - That table DOES NOT EXIST in the live database. Direct query of information_schema returns exactly one table in the public schema: items. Selecting from rate_limit_hits returns 'relation "rate_limit_hits" does not exist'.
  - It is not created lazily: I posted an item, then re-queried, and the table was still absent.
  - package.json defines "migrate": "node migrations/run.mjs", but NOTHING invokes it as part of a deploy. "build" is plain "next build", and there is no vercel.json. So the migration is committed but was never applied to the database this app actually talks to.
  - With the store missing, every limiter call throws, and Req 6's fail-open path swallows it and allows the request. The feature is therefore permanently open in exactly the way Req 6 intends only as a temporary safety net.

This is the same SHAPE as sprint 1's statically-rendered health endpoint and sprint 1's "Other" framework preset: the code is plausibly correct and the deployed environment does not carry what it needs. It is invisible to a static audit - QA1 was right that the store is shared and not in-process, which is what Req 2 asks of the CODE - and it is invisible to any local test, because a laptop runs the migration. It is only visible by posting ten times at the real URL, which is the criterion Req 2 was written to force.

Fails Req 1 (limit not enforced), Req 2 (no shared state in play at all), Req 3 (no 429, no Retry-After ever emitted).

=======================================================================
DEFECT 2 - LOWER SEVERITY. The honeypot announces itself.
=======================================================================
Req 5 requires the honeypot rejection be "indistinguishable to the client from an ordinary validation failure"; QA1's own criterion says "identical to an ordinary validation rejection." It is neither.
  honeypot 'company' filled -> HTTP 400 {"error":"Request could not be processed."}
I swept every other rejection the endpoint produces to check whether that string is shared by any legitimate path. It is not - twelve other rejections, twelve different messages, none of them this one:
  empty title / whitespace title / empty body -> "Title is required."
  long title        -> "Title must be 200 characters or fewer."
  negative price    -> "Price cannot be negative."
  price "abc"       -> "Price must be a valid number."
  price 100001      -> "Price cannot exceed $100,000."
  price null        -> "Price is required."
  missing/empty email -> "Email is required."
  bad email shape   -> "Email does not look like a valid address."
  malformed JSON    -> "Request body must be valid JSON."
  HONEYPOT          -> "Request could not be processed."   <-- unique
A bot that submits once with the field filled and once without learns immediately which field is the trap, and simply stops filling it. That defeats the honeypot's only mechanism. The status code matches (400) but the body does not, and the requirement is about the response, not the status alone.

=======================================================================
BLOCKED BY DEFECT 1 - NOT TESTED, AND NOT AN ENVIRONMENT PROBLEM
=======================================================================
These three cannot be evaluated while the limiter allows everything. There is no environment to arrange and no permission to grant - the limiter has to work before any of them means anything. I am naming them explicitly so none is mistaken for passing:

  Req 2 (cross-instance): the criterion asks for requests spaced to span serverless instances. Spanning instances is meaningless when a single burst from one instance is not limited either. Untested.

  Req 3 (429 + sane Retry-After): no 429 was ever produced, so there was no Retry-After value to inspect. Untested.

  Req 7 (bucket not choosable by the client): THIS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST, and it is the reason the sprint file was amended after QA1's round-1 BLOCKING finding. The amendment exists specifically because the append-versus-replace question about Vercel's edge "cannot be settled by a static read at all - only requirement 7's new live criterion can settle it." That live criterion is exactly what Defect 1 prevents from running: varying x-forwarded-for, x-real-ip and x-vercel-forwarded-for cannot demonstrate that the limit holds when the limit does not hold for an unvarying client either. Every request is allowed regardless of headers, so the measurement returns no information. The open question the amendment raised is still open, and no implementation may depend on its answer until it has been measured. Re-run this the moment the limiter is live.

=======================================================================
PASSING - verified, and re-verify after the fix since some interact
=======================================================================
Req 5 (hiding technique): PASS, and I measured it rather than trusting the markup. The 'company' field renders at left: -9999px, 4x4 px, insideViewport false, with aria-hidden="true", tabindex="-1", autocomplete="off" and no associated label. That is the off-screen-plus-aria-hidden technique the requirement asks for, not a bare type="hidden" and not visually-hidden-but-announced. NOTE ON MY OWN MEASUREMENT: a first pass reported visibleToUser:true and I did not report it - that was an artifact of using offsetWidth, which is non-zero for an off-screen element. Measuring the bounding rect is what settles it, and it is off-screen.
Req 5 (no row created): PASS. Board row count before and after the honeypot submissions: 10 and 10.
Req 5 (honeypot does not break real posting): PASS, and this is the quiet failure mode the sprint file warns about, so I tested it in a real browser rather than by API. Filling the visible form in headless Chromium produced HTTP 201, the item count went 13 -> 14, and the new item appeared in the DOM. Ordinary posting through the real form works.
Req 4 (three ordinary posts not blocked): PASS as observed - three successive posts all returned 201. Flagging honestly that this result is currently VACUOUS: nothing is being blocked, so it demonstrates nothing about whether the chosen 5/hour policy accommodates normal use. Re-run it once the limiter actually enforces.
Req 6 (fail-open when the store is unavailable): PASS, demonstrated - though by accident rather than by the intended test. The production state right now IS the store-unavailable state, and posting continues to work rather than failing closed. That is precisely the behaviour Req 6 specifies, observed under real conditions. Two caveats: I did not reach it via the intended poisoned-preview route, and I could NOT confirm the required server-side logging - a query of the deployment's runtime events returned no usable log lines, which is inconclusive about whether the failure is logged, not evidence that it is not. Re-verify the logging separately.
Req 8 (sprint 2 validation intact): PASS. Empty title -> 400 "Title is required."; negative price -> 400 "Price cannot be negative."; missing email -> 400 "Email is required."; price "abc" -> 400 "Price must be a valid number." No rows created by any.

=======================================================================
NOTES
=======================================================================
WORKTREE / SHARED DATABASE, worth knowing before the fix: this branch preview shares ONE Neon database with production. I proved it rather than assuming - an item posted to the preview URL (id 22) appeared immediately on the production board. Two consequences. First, my rate-limit test rows landed on the real production board, and I have cleaned them up. Second, and more important for the fix: running the migration against that database will affect production and the preview together, and the rate_limit_hits table currently being absent means the limiter is doing nothing on PRODUCTION too, not only on this preview. Sprint 4 shipped to production on commit 07a453e and this gap is live there right now.

PARALLEL-WORK BOUNDARY RESPECTED: the sprint's own diff touches app/api/items/route.ts, components/board.tsx, lib/client-ip.ts, lib/rate-limit.ts, lib/rate-limit-window.ts, lib/spam-guard.ts, migrations/0002, tests, package.json and tsconfig.json. It does not touch lib/items.ts or app/claim/**, which belong to sprint 4.

WHAT THE FIX NEEDS TO COVER: applying the migration is necessary but is not by itself the whole fix - a migration that must be run by hand after every deploy will be missed again. Whatever mechanism is chosen (a build-time migrate step, a release command, an idempotent ensure-table on first use), the thing that must become true is that a fresh deploy of this app to a fresh database ends up with rate_limit_hits present without a human remembering. That is Dev Team 2's call to make and QA1's to audit, not mine to design.

AFTER THE FIX, RE-RUN AT MINIMUM: Req 1/3 (exceed the limit, confirm 429 + Retry-After, confirm no rows), Req 2 (spaced requests spanning instances, reporting count and period), Req 7 (the full header-variation matrix, and report the header values the deployed app actually received so the append-versus-replace question is finally answered with evidence), Req 4 (non-vacuously this time), and Req 6's logging.
